oneSentence: Recorded observations, measurements or examples that people or systems can store, examine and use for a purpose.
plainExplanation:
Data is the raw material many digital systems work with. It can be numbers, words, images, sound, locations, dates or labels. A single item might be a temperature reading, a line of text or a photo.

What goes in depends on the task. A person, sensor, form or computer system records observations or events. Those records are then stored, organised, checked, combined or cleaned, which means fixing obvious errors and putting them into a usable form.

What comes out can be many things. People may produce a chart, a list, a report or a decision with human review. An AI system may use data to find patterns, make a prediction or generate text, but the output depends strongly on the quality and relevance of the data it receives.

Data is not the same as a dataset. Data can mean one item or many kinds of recorded information, while a dataset usually means a specific collection prepared for analysis or training. Data is also not the same as metadata, which is data about data, such as when a file was created or who entered a record.

everydayAnalogy.title: Notes on slips of paper before a meeting
everydayAnalogy.story: Before a community meeting in Lima, Sofia asks volunteers to write one transport problem per slip of paper. Some slips say "bus late", some say "road flooded", and some include times and neighbourhood names. The team sorts the slips into groups, removes duplicates and corrects a few spelling mistakes so they can count the main issues. After that, they can make a summary for the meeting agenda.

mapping.analogyElement: each slip of paper with one problem written on it
times and neighbourhood names on the slips
mapping.aiElement: different features or fields in the data

mapping.analogyElement: sorting, deduplicating and correcting the slips
mapping.aiElement: organising and cleaning data before use
an output such as an analysis, report or model input

everydayAnalogy.limitation: Real data systems can handle millions of records automatically and may include images, audio or sensor readings, not just short written notes. Also, unlike slips of paper, digital data can be copied, linked and reused very easily, which creates governance, privacy and security issues the analogy does not show.

visual.title: From observation to usable output
visual.learningObjective: Show that data starts as recorded observations, is prepared through several steps, and then becomes usable for analysis, reporting or AI tasks.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. Box 1 shows sources: a form icon, a sensor icon and a document icon. Box 2 shows recorded items as small cards containing examples such as a number, a date, a word and an image thumbnail. Box 3 shows preparation actions with labels: store, organise, clean, label. Box 4 shows outputs with icons for a chart, a report and an AI model input tray. Each arrow has a short label: collect, prepare, use.

steps.label: Observe or record
steps.explanation: Information begins as something noticed or measured by a person or system.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw source icons grouped in the first box: clipboard form, thermometer sensor and document page.

steps.label: Create data items
steps.explanation: Each observation becomes a stored item such as a row, file, message or image.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw small cards in the second box with sample contents: '27°C', '12 May', 'bridge closed', and a simple image placeholder.

steps.label: Prepare the data
steps.explanation: Items are stored, organised and cleaned so they can be used reliably.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw the third box with four small action chips labelled 'store', 'organise', 'clean', 'label'.

steps.label: Use the data
steps.explanation: Prepared data can support analysis, reporting or AI systems.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw the final box with three outputs: bar chart, short report page and a tray labelled 'model input'.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap, each box reveals one example sentence: source example, data item example, preparation example and output example.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This diagram explains data as a process. First, information comes from sources such as forms, sensors or documents. Second, each observation is recorded as a data item, for example a temperature value, a date, a short text note or an image. Third, the items are prepared by storing them, organising them, cleaning errors and sometimes adding labels. Fourth, the prepared data is used to create outputs such as charts, reports or input for an AI model. The main message is that data is recorded information that becomes useful only after preparation for a specific purpose.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flow chart shows the same sequence without animation: sources, recorded items, preparation actions and outputs, with labelled arrows reading collect, prepare and use.

workedExample.scenario: A phone keyboard feature is built to suggest the next word in short messages.
workedExample.input: Example training text includes lines such as: “see you tomorrow”, “see you soon”, “thank you”, “thank you very much” and “are you coming”.
process: The text examples are encoded and stored as data.
The system divides the text into smaller units, called tokens, and records which tokens tend to occur together.
From the examples, it identifies that some words follow “thank you” more often than others.
When a user types “thank you”, the system uses those learned patterns to rank possible next words.
workedExample.result: The feature suggests the continuation that its data makes most likely. Different or newly collected data could produce a different ranking.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A communications officer at a field office with an unreliable connection is serving on a recruitment panel. Before the panel meets at close of business, she exports the applications from the approved recruitment system and records each candidate’s evidence against the rostered profile in a selection matrix.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The exported fields, application text and entries in the selection matrix are all data: recorded observations and labels encoded as table cells or text. Their usefulness depends on consistent criteria, accurate transcription and enough context for the panel to interpret them properly.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Applicant details and assessment notes are personal and HR-sensitive. They must not be pasted into an external or unapproved AI tool, because doing so could disclose personal information and compromise the selection process. Use only approved systems, restrict access and handle the file under the applicable retention and confidentiality instructions.

whyItMatters: If you hear claims about AI, dashboards or evidence-based decisions, the first practical question is what data was used. Good decisions need relevant, lawful and well-managed data; poor or biased data can produce misleading outputs even when the software looks impressive.
whereYouMayHearIt: A recruitment panel agreeing the fields in a selection matrix
A vendor demo to an ICT governance board
An inter-agency working group reviewing a needs assessment
A programme review before a monitoring report is cleared
A data protection briefing before access is granted to a new platform

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Data only means numbers in a spreadsheet.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Numbers are one kind of data, but text, images, audio, locations and timestamps can also be data if they are recorded and used for a purpose.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More data always gives better results.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Quantity helps only if the data is relevant and of sufficient quality. Large amounts of outdated, biased or inaccurate data can make results worse.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Data and dataset mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Data is a broad term for recorded information. A dataset usually means a defined collection of data assembled for a task such as analysis or model training.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Data is recorded information that a person or computer can use.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Data consists of encoded observations, measurements or labels represented in a form that can be stored, processed and transmitted, such as rows in a table, text tokens, image pixels or sensor values.

keyTakeaway: Data is recorded material in a usable form. What a system can show or learn depends on what was recorded, how it was encoded and how it was prepared.

quickCheck.question: Which option best describes data in an AI context?
options: Only numerical values stored in a spreadsheet
Recorded information such as text, images, measurements or labels that a system can use
The final answer produced by an AI system
A rule that tells software exactly what to do
quickCheck.explanation: Data is the input material: recorded information in many forms. A final answer is an output, and a rule is part of an algorithm or software design. Restricting data to spreadsheets is too narrow.

issues.problem: Calling data "facts" incorrectly implies that recorded data is true. Data can contain errors, false claims, uncertain labels or inaccurate measurements.
issues.fix: Recorded observations, measurements or examples that people or systems can store, examine and use for a purpose.

issues.problem: The objective states that data always starts as recorded observations. Data can also be derived, generated or transformed from other data.
issues.fix: Show how observations can be recorded as data, prepared through several steps, and used for analysis, reporting or AI tasks.

issues.problem: The final sentence says data becomes useful only after preparation. Some data can be used as recorded, without cleaning, labelling or other preparation.
issues.fix: Replace the final sentence with: "The main message is that recorded information can be used directly or prepared for a specific purpose."

issues.problem: The meeting summary maps naturally to an analysis or report, but not to a model input. Adding model input here does not match the story and blurs inputs with outputs.
issues.fix: an output such as an analysis or report

issues.problem: The diagram groups a chart, a report and an AI model input under "outputs". Model input is not an output of the AI model. It can be an output of preparation, but the diagram does not identify that boundary.
issues.fix: Call Box 4 "uses" rather than "outputs", and show a chart, a report and data entering an AI model.

issues.problem: The takeaway incorrectly defines data only as input material. A system can also produce data, and one system's output can become another system's input.
issues.fix: Data is recorded material, not only input; system results depend heavily on what was recorded and how it was prepared.

issues.problem: Option 2 is the only general definition. Option 1 is too narrow, option 3 names only one possible source of data, and option 4 describes an instruction. However, the explanation creates a false input-output divide: an AI answer is an output, but it can become data if recorded and used.
issues.fix: Data is recorded information in many forms. An AI answer can later become data, but it is not a general definition. A rule is a software instruction, and spreadsheets are only one format.

voicePass.note: Improved workplace specificity, removed invented statistics, and strengthened HR-data safeguards.
